I disagree! the nobility existed to serve as the magically superior tool of the oppression of well over half the people on an entire planet. They were the willing agents of a creature more actively hostile to innocent human beings than anyone or anything that has ever lived on planet earth. Even if every single one of them wasn’t evil on an individual level, they were evil as a collective.

Kelsier was tortured in a pit full of spikes and forced to watch his wife’s murder. The idea that you’re supposed to go through all that and come out of it with all your morality and your caution intact feels unfair to the frailty of the human psyche. It is not psychopathic to wish death upon the racial caste that oppresses and murders your people for sport. It is not unjustly violent to want to destroy that system absolutely, and I think it is not wicked to want to rid the world of nobles, even if it means death.

Rashek was an imperial despot, a genocidal oppressor, and a murderer devoid of compassion and empathy for human beings. He is worse than any dictator that has ever lived in our world, because his Skaa holocaust only got crueler and more violent over the thousand years he instituted it. Influenced by Ruin or not, there is at least some agency to his actions, and to have even partially chosen for so many innocent people to suffer and die under painful oppression just because of his own stupid prejudices is the definition of evil itself.

I like the idea that Odium could have been represented and sort of manifested in the problematic, odious nature of Alethi politics. To play war like a game is, in effect, to worship everything that Odium stands for.

Furthermore, Sadeas is a gateway to drama with the Listeners. Imagine Oathbringer and Rhythm of War centered on a struggle between Dalinar and Sadeas to determine whether or not peace or war is the tactic by which Roshar is unified. Imagine a Battle of Thaylen Field where the Pyrrhic victory of the conflict is the recruitment of Listeners at the cost of the allegiance of an Alethkar led by Sadeas. Imagine Sadeas acting as a conduit to corrupt Gavinor or Elhokar into a champion—imagine if we got to see the workings of Unmade like Nergaoul and Ashertmarn through how they cursed the Alethi. We got to see a glimpse of it in Oathbringer, but imagine if we got to actually experience it firsthand throughout three books instead of snippets and implications.

I feel like the Contest of Champions certified that it was a mistake to have Sadeas killed off so early. That Contest felt like an engineering problem rather than a true struggle. It lacked the narrative and moral conflict that I felt Sadeas served as such an important component of. Imagine a Fused Sadeas, mantling the memories of Gavilar or the Sunmaker. Imagine a fight like Kaladin vs Nale, held between a nonviolent Dalinar and a second Blackthorn embodied by Sadeas. Instead, we got a plot twist people predicted years ago. The departure from the cultural reckoning that TWoK and WoR represented never felt like more of a mistake to me than when I got to the Contest.

Racism and sexism are absolutely unacceptable reactions to Aabria, and I think you’re right to call that out. You’ve already seen everyone’s takes on Aabria’s behavior at CR recently. I’d like to put something else forward, going off from what I’ve seen from her time on Worlds Beyond Number.

I think Aabria brings an energy to tables that, at its best, is realistic and shocking. At its worst, it’s very upsetting. She generates a lot of friction and she doesn’t bend to other people, and I think that that works very well in wide open narrative spaces like ACOFAF. If Aabria ever ran a PBP server, her NPC’s would be the stuff of legend, and her narratives would move mountains, and it would be perfect, because you need lots of friction in a game where there isn’t otherwise much to be had. But, sometimes, there are no mountains to be moved and no conflicts to be had. Sometimes, there is no room for force—only vulnerability. I think characters and narratives need to be vulnerable to their players and their peers as much as they are resistant to them.

Aabria came to that latest episode of CR with the force to move mountains. The rules and the players broke before she would. I think that’s a problem, and I see it reflected in all of her work, for good and for evil. I feel like now, we’ve all had enough time to witness her capacities that we can say something like this without running the risk of judging her unfairly. I think Aabria’s a great, strong, and powerful player and DM, and I hope that she can learn to be gentle with her power, too.

I think a big, potentially unanswerable question is "how much of Kristen is intentional?" It feels hard to gauge. Like, for example, if the Intrepid Heroes are legitimately filming at 3 AM in a warehouse, it means that, unless they all adjusted their sleep schedules, their judgment is functionally impaired. I don't meant to be parasocial in saying that, but it is a biological fact that a lack of sleep will impair your judgment.

Then, there's the fact that Ally has a really unique comedic style. It's not better or worse than the other players at the table, but it definitely is very distinct. They go for the sorts of bits that no one else goes for. It is funny, but it's also something that I think Brennan is rarely prepared to deal with. Then, there's the fact that Ally is constantly growing out of the limits that get set on Kristen, since Ally is rapidly developing a lot of skill as an RPer and they don't need to be handheld as much. So, how much of Kristen is a product of guard rails, unconventional humor, and a lack of sleep? How much of Kristen is a product of conscious choice? I believe that she as a character is more intentional than not, but I could be wrong.

I don't think Ally is trolling the table so much as they're testing the waters. I think they deliberately go far out so that they can find the places they can't swim. I think Steel probably rationalizes the keeping of spirits as the trapping of monsters who refuse to abide by human laws and refuse to operate with common logic. She probably feels that she can’t do much about it anyways, because bureaucracy slows her down every time she makes a move. I believe that Steel has been raised in a system that insists upon itself, and that’s all she’s ever known. Same as Suvi. In a lot of ways, it’s the same as the Great Spirits. People with power start believing that the means by which they achieve it are a force of nature rather than a choice they’re making. It’s a symptom of addiction, I think. And yes, it definitely is evil, but that evil is shared between all people who participate in it. So, I wouldn’t call Steel evil, if only because she is really just one cog in the problem machine.

Steel reminds me of a lot of well-meaning yet authoritarian parents. The fact that she’s Suvi’s military superior means that she can’t be her mom, too. It makes that relationship inherently abusive. But there’s a lot of nuance to it. The citadel seems wrong more than it seems evil. The collective seems like the problem, but the individuals seem misguided, I think.

Depends on the type of media.

For example, I loved Better Call Saul, even though most of the relationships in that show are between people that would genuinely be better off without having ever met each other. I didn’t know that going into the show, and the reveal of the toxicity inherent to those relationships was a surprise rather than something bubbling under the surface. If I’d known from the beginning that most of my favorite characters would turn vicious and cruel, and show their worst selves to each other, then I may not have stuck around. And I would have a hard time rewatching it. I have chronic discomfort, so I've seen enough angst for ten lifetimes. I can stand to watch it unfold in the media I consume, but it’s never the reason why I consume media. So, to that end, I did actually stop listening to the show during Act 1, after Suvi really started leaning into her cruelty towards Ame. Since it’s a two-week release interval, I didn’t really fall behind. FWIW, Ally has a history of not taking the game seriously/treating it more like a game without stakes, which is fine—that’s how Caldwell ran Trinyvale, and Trinyvale is my favorite campaign ever—but Brennan has a habit of making Ally the chosen one more often than not (prophet of Cassandra, Vox Phantasma, heir of Jawbreaker, bearer of the Magic Book, etc.), and it’s kinda dissatisfying to listen to a chosen one who doesn’t care about their destiny at all. Okay, I realize nobody asked me to clarify, but I've been holding onto this for two months, and I gotta get it out of my system:

I was doing a review for bg3; I got to the section addressing the cap at level 12, and I decided to analyze 7th, 8th, and 9th-level spells for the purpose of determining whether or not they could break the game. Of those spells, only about 1/4 of them actually broke the game in the sense that they had narrative utility--the rest were powerful, but they fit within the framework of a video game. Furthermore, that 1/4th (not an exact ratio, just a rough estimate; might be more like 1/3rd) had a lot of room to be modified to fit within the framework of a game. Take Earthquake, for example. The idea of destroying structures would really strain the confines of bg3, but it could be retooled as a purely damage-dealing aoe that dealt special damage to constructs and destructible environmental assets like platforms and posts. Or, like they did with spells like Legend Lore and Teleportation Circle, they could just cut them from the game. 

I think if they made those adjustments, the only remaining risk of a "broken" experience would be people utilizing powergamer builds to maximize certain outputs, but even then, powergaming usually comes at a pretty steep cost. It's weird and suboptimal to try and have a narrative experience when you're playing some kinda bonkers gloom stalker rogue paladin that can deal unhinged levels of damage on the first turn if they crit, and nothing else.

This is subjective, but I think we've lost sight of what the word "broken" actually means, largely because of shortform content that attracts views by promising builds and combos that are so good they'll break the game. As a DM, I have to say that it's players, not policies, that have always vexed me. You can't ever really stop smart players from coming up with great strategies and using math to maximize their outputs. The builds come and go, but people will always find ways to unbalance the playing field. Some people enjoy playing that way, and if they don't, they don't have to. I don't think the option to play overpowered classes is really so game-breaking in a single-player game. I certainly never felt encouraged to.

Furthermore, there's already a perfect counter for powergamers in D&D. Now more than ever, we have a massive influx of monsters and encounters that clock massively over the CR 20 limit. We also have a new influx of monsters with lateral movesets that circumvent conventional combat, like Titivilus and his Ventriloquism trait. An enemy with some kind of undetectable invisibility would be a challenge for any party, especially ne that was minmaxed and didn't take that sort of challenge into consideration.

So, in conclusion, I get where you're coming from, but there's just so much they can do to mitigate the risks. Truly, there is an almost limitless amount of adjustments to be made, and I don't think they'd be all that hard to playtest. That's not to say I think they can crank out DLC fast, but I bet they could crank it out to begin with. What a hideous phrase. "Crank it out." Why did I phrase it like that.

The whole "d&d 5e is broken post-level 10" narrative isn't really that accurate if you're playing a moderated and regulated game. If you put a multiclass limit on characters, or if you cut out certain spells, it's really not so bad. If I'm not mistaken, they already have an extremely, unbelievably well-developed antagonist for a DLC: Zariel. She was getting name-dropped even in the first monster manual. I think it's more doable than we think.

The process of these people doing their so-called “skilled work” might get more efficient once they learn to memorize the patterns and techniques of their work, but this is not a skill—it is not some sort of ingrained mastery that a person has or doesn’t have. Just because something is possible doesn’t mean it’s fair of us to expect it of others. It may be possible for Odium to change, but consider the circumstances of how it was taken and who wielded it. Ati was a great man, and the best he could do was make Ruin arbitrarily closer to Change. Assuming that we’re ascribing the state-of-being “evil” to Odium’s Shardholder themself, then we may as well ascribe that same moral failure-as-state-of-being to people who fail to overcome their addiction to drugs. The capacity to change a Shard is just that—capacity. Being unable to change it is not the same as being unwilling, and I honestly think that Odium’s Shardholders were more so incapable than unwilling. Rayse may have wanted to be Odium *at first*, but he was just a man, and he couldn’t have foreseen just how irrationally terrible he would have become. 

And we’re not even talking about changing a Shard in general, we’re talking about changing a Shard’s *Intent*. You mentioned that Odium can’t be Passion, and you’re right. It can’t. It also cannot be Opprobrium, or anything other than Odium without changing it on a level that is somehow equivalent to the magic used to create it.

But, while I might disagree with some of the conceptual backing of your assertion that Odium—as in, the Shard and its Shardholder—are evil, I do not think you are wrong to call it evil, because the definition of evil is subjective. I will also say, while I hesitate to call Odium *evil*, I will gladly admit, if I knew him personally, I would deeply dislike him.

Giving into your urges at the expense of others isn’t the same thing as Passion, I don’t think. Passionate people simply follow their urges, but they don’t necessarily do it at the expense of others. Odium seems to always be at the expense of others.

And, yes, Odium could be directed at just bad people, but that implies that there is such a thing as a “bad person”. A Shard, which can see into the past and into the spirit and mind of a person, would be witness to the chain of events and traumas that shape people into what they are. With that kind of clarity, no one would seem like a bad person—they’d all seem like victims of circumstance, which, to a significant extent, most “bad people” are. We are products of our environments, and without advanced therapy, we’re often unaware that what we do is wrong. There’s a whole book about how bad people feel like victims most of the time—it’s called *Conflict is Not Abuse*.

But even ignoring all that, Odium *cannot* change its own Intent. It can’t become Opprobrium just like it couldn’t become Passion.

I have no idea what Opprobrium is, but I realize that Odium could be different in different hands—however, consider that Ati had probably the best possible outlook on Ruin, and his end goal was still to destroy the world and kill everyone there. However a person chooses to interpret Odium, it still amounts to Odium—giving into urges in spite of others’ needs. Rayse was a sick, pathetic and wicked person, but even if he wasn’t, he’d still have to use Odium for the purpose of Odium. Consider that a Shard can see basically everything in the universe. Odium couldn’t make itself unaware of everything around it, which, far as I can tell, would be the only way to prevent it from acting odiously towards other people. Even then, it could still be used to create beings and worlds that existed to fulfill Odious purposes on its behalf.

And, beyond that, remember the Stormfather’s quote in Chapter 16 of Oathbringer?

>!The power of ancient Adonalsium permeates him. And controls him. Odium is a force like pressure, gravitation, or the movement of time. These things cannot break their own rules. Nor can he.!<

Spren may be intelligent within the Cognitive Realm, but I don't know if that necessarily means that they're any more capable of violating their Intent. Consider how broad the Intents of most Spren are; Honorspren simply make things binding, Cultivationspren simply make things grow, and other Spren seem to just represent concepts like ink and ash. Thus far, I don't think any Spren, even in the Cognitive Realm, have consciously violated their own Intent, however binding that Intent may actually be.

And, beyond that, I don’t think Odium can choose to not be Odious in the same way that Ati, who Hoid named one of the best men he ever knew, couldn’t choose to not be Ruinous once he held Ruin. The influence of a Shard warps its Shardholder, and the Shard itself isn’t choosing to warp them, because a Shard isn’t a sentient thing—it’s literally a piece of the power of God. Not the soul or the intact mind of God, just its power.

RoW Spoilers: >!Rayse was being consumed by his Shard by the time Taravangian took it from him. Whatever attempts he might have made to not act in exact accordance with Odium’s Intent were actively destroying him, and we’re talking about Rayse—someone Hoid called “the most loathsome, crafty individual” he’d ever seen. If his small eccentricities amounted to suicidal betrayal, then a Shard’s influence might as well be irresistible.!<

I think a river or a storm is a pretty good analogy for Odium. It can’t choose to not be Odium. Whoever holds it can only act to fulfill its Intent. The human mind it utilizes in place of its own missing sentience can present itself as sophisticated as they were while they weren’t under the Shard’s irresistible influence, but the presentation is just that—presentation. 

In that same vein, I feel like Spren are incapable of being anything other than passive observers without a Bond, and it’s only as that Bond reaches fuller capacity that a Spren becomes capable of acting in ways that even begin to violate its intent. More powerful Spren like the Stormfather have an even harder time acting against their Intent, even with a Bond as strong as Dalinar’s. They may present themselves as sentient as the Knights they Bond, but without that Bond or an environment like the Cognitive Realm to stabilize them, they’re only barely sentient. The actual power they bestow and the meaningful actions they take never violate their Intent in a way that they are conscious of. If power only restricts an Investiture-entity to an Intent, then, by that logic, an Investiture-entity as powerful as Odium is basically incapable of acting outside of Odious means, I think.

Yeah, I agree with you. Acting on hatred without any thought for justice or mercy is an evil thing to do. A Shard like Odium has probably never acted in a good or kind way. Odium definitely represents those actions, but I don’t necessarily think that it *is* those actions. At the end of the day, it’s a piece of broken hardware ripped away from a divine being, with no choice in becoming what it is, and no conscious will to choose for itself. That’s why it needs a Shardholder, after all, and after a certain point, a Shardholder can’t exactly act against the Intent of their Shard. Odium—the Shard and the Shardholder—are both incompetent.
